docs.title: Introduction and RuleSet Features
docs.text: RuleSet is a data validation language that non-coding domain experts can use to develop, maintain, and communicate data validation rules. The accompanying data validation program, ruleset-engine, validates a data table against rules written in RuleSet.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Atomic Rules — Each rule in RuleSet targets a single feature of your dataset. For instance, applying an "is not null" rule to a column will solely check for the presence of null values, without performing any type or format validations.

  • Rule Stacking — You can specify multiple atomic rules for a data column. Rules are evaluated independently, and their order does not affect the outcome. A data column must pass all applicable rules to be considered valid. Successful validations are recorded with an "all OK" message in the log file.

  • Rule Blocks — If a group of columns share the same rules, RuleSet allows you to define those rules once and apply them to the entire group. Rules that are specific to individual columns can still be defined separately.

  • Conditional Validation — RuleSet supports conditional validations, which let you apply validation rules only when a condition is met. For example: if column A contains "John Doe," then column B must contain "1970-12-22." You may specify multiple consequent rules, e.g. if column country is "USA" then column State must be in ["CO", "NY", "FL"]; column Zip Code must be an integer and have 5 digits.

  • No implicit evaluation — Data is never evaluated implicitly. All validation rules must be explicitly defined to be applied.

  • No data modification — Data is never modified during the validation process.

With these features, RuleSet lets you specify data validation rules at different levels of stringency — from a quick type check on every column, to fully conditional, cross-column business rules. The Rules File and Data File pages walk through a complete worked example.

docs.title: Data File
docs.text: The data file is the actual table being validated against your rules file.

docs.title: Accepted formats
docs.text: ruleset-engine accepts .csv, .tsv, and .xls/.xlsx format data files. Data files are expected to be tabular with column headers included in the first row.

docs.title: What happens if the format is incorrect
docs.text:
If ruleset-engine cannot read the data file at all — an unsupported file type, a corrupted file, or a path that doesn't resolve — it writes an error to the log file explaining what went wrong (e.g. Error: could not read data file. <underlying error>) and exits without attempting any validation. It does not partially validate a file it couldn't fully parse, and it never modifies or attempts to repair the data file itself.

This is distinct from a data file that parses successfully but fails individual rules (a wrong value type, a null in a required column, and so on) — those are reported per-column as validation errors in the log, not as a file-format error. See Section 5.6 for how each case is logged.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install ruleset-engine

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
ruleset-engine --rules-file RULES_FILE --data-file DATA_FILE [--logfile-path LOGFILE_PATH]

Required Arguments: - --rules-file RULES_FILE — Path to the file containing the data validation rules (see Section 3). - --data-file DATA_FILE — Path to the data file to be validated (see Section 4).

Optional Arguments: - --logfile-path LOGFILE_PATH — Directory path where the log file will be stored. If not specified, the current working directory is used. - -h, --help — Display the help message and exit.

Notes: - Ensure the ruleset-engine command is on your system's PATH (a standard pip install handles this automatically). - Logfile names include a timestamp: YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_ruleset.log. - See Section 5.6 for a full explanation of log output, with examples.

docs.title: A minimal end-to-end example
docs.text:
ruleset-engine --rules-file squash_rules.ruleset --data-file top_15_squash_players.csv

The Rules File and Data File pages build out exactly this squash_rules.ruleset / top_15_squash_players.csv pair in detail.

docs.title: Rules File
docs.text: A rules file is a plain-text file containing one or more RuleSet rules. It has no required file extension — .ruleset, .dsl, or no extension at all are all valid, since ruleset-engine only cares about the file's contents, not its name.

docs.title: Correct format
docs.text:
• Lines starting with // are comments and are ignored; comments may appear anywhere in the file.
  • Every rules file must contain exactly one column names in [ … ] rule — this is the only required rule in RuleSet (see Section 5.2).
  • Beyond that, rules are composed from the building blocks in Section 5: global settings, column rules, value rules, rule blocks, and conditional rules — combined in whatever order and combination your validation needs call for.
  • Rule order does not affect the validation outcome (see Rule Stacking, Section 1).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Here's a complete, valid rules file. It validates a table of squash players: every column has a declared type, PSA_ID must be unique and start with 'PSA', Country must be one of nine listed values, and a conditional rule handles the fact that UK postal codes (Wales, England) are alphanumeric while other countries' zip codes are numeric.

//Rules to validate top_15_squash_players.csv
//Column ID should be unique; each value should start with 'PSA'; PSA0000 is not a valid value.
//Column Country can have only one of the following values:
//'EGY', 'PER', 'NZL', 'IND', 'MAS', 'WAL', 'ENG', 'FRA', 'SUI'.
//Column Year_of_Birth should have the format 'YYYY'.
//Column Zip_Code is not null.
//Conditional rules:
//Zip_Code for Wales and England should be of type string.
//Zip_Code for all other countries should be of type integer.
//-------------------------------------

column names in ['Rank', 'PSA_ID', 'First_Name', 'Last_Name', 'Country', 'Year_of_Birth', 'Address', 'Zip_Code']
all columns required
no extra columns allowed

column: 'Rank'
has value type integer
is > 0

column: 'PSA_ID'
has value type string
is unique
starts with 'PSA'
is not 'PSA0000'

column: 'First_Name'
has value type string

column: 'Last_Name'
has value type string

column: 'Country'
has value type string
is in ['EGY', 'PER', 'NZL', 'IND', 'MAS', 'WAL', 'ENG', 'FRA', 'SUI']

column: 'Year_of_Birth'
has value type date-time
has format 'YYYY'

column: 'Address'
has value type string

column: 'Zip_Code'
is not null

"WalesEnglandZipCodeRule"
if
column: 'Country' is in ['WAL', 'ENG']
then
column: 'Zip_Code' has value type string

"NotWalesEnglandZipCodeRule"
if
column: 'Country' is not in ['WAL', 'ENG']
then
column: 'Zip_Code' has value type integer

This same example is referenced throughout Section 5 when individual syntax features are explained.

docs.title: RuleSet Syntax
docs.text:
This section is the full syntax reference for RuleSet, split into:

  • Global Settings
  • Column Rules
  • Value Rules
  • Rule Blocks
  • Conditional Validation
  • The Log File

docs.title: Column Rules
docs.text: Specify which columns must be included, whether all named columns are required, and whether extra columns are allowed.

docs.title: column names in [ … ]
docs.text:
Description: (Required) List exactly which columns the table must contain. This is the only required rule in RuleSet — every rules file must have a column names list. Syntax:

column names in <list of column names>

Example:

column names in ['user_id', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'signup_date']

docs.title: all columns required
docs.text:
Description: Fail if any of the named columns is missing. Syntax & Example:

all columns required

docs.title: no extra columns allowed
docs.text:
Description: Fail if the data table contains any column not listed in the rules file. Syntax & Example:

no extra columns allowed

docs.title: check column order
docs.text:
Description: Physical column order must match the order listed in the rules file. Syntax & Example:

check column order

docs.title: Conditional Validation
docs.text:
Apply a rule only when a condition (if) is met. The consequent (then) can include multiple atomic rules, each applied to a separate column. Multiple if/then rules can be specified in one rules file. Each conditional rule needs a rule tag (a quoted string identifying it).

Syntax:

<Rule Tag> if
column: <ColumnA> <ValueRuleA>
then
column: <ColumnB> <ValueRuleB>
column: <ColumnC> <ValueRuleC>

Example:

'USAStateZipRule' if
column: 'country' is "USA"
then
column: 'zipcode' has pattern /^\d{5}(-\d{4})?$/
column: 'state' in ['MD', 'NY', 'DE', 'VA']

The worked example in Section 3 uses two conditional rules together (WalesEnglandZipCodeRule and NotWalesEnglandZipCodeRule) to apply different Zip_Code type rules depending on Country.

docs.title: Global Settings
docs.text: Global dataset settings that apply across the whole rules file (not to any one column).

docs.title: allowed null values in [ … ]
docs.text:
Description: Treat the listed literals as null/missing values. Syntax:

allowed null values in <list of literals to be treated as null>

Example:

allowed null values in ["Not Measured", "Not Collected", "Not Included", "-"]

docs.title: thousands separator is "…"
docs.text:
Description: Specify the character used to separate thousands in numeric fields. Syntax:

thousands separator is <seperator>

Example:

thousands separator is "."

docs.title: set tolerance at <NUMBER>
docs.text:
Description: Specify the tolerance level used for numeric comparisons. The default is 0.001 — two values are considered equal if they differ by no more than that. Setting tolerance at this level applies it globally to all numeric comparisons in the rules file. You can also specify tolerance for an individual comparison (see Section 5.3); when both a global and a local tolerance are defined, the local tolerance takes precedence. Syntax:

set tolerance at <tolerance level>

Example:

set tolerance at 0.00001
set tolerance at 1E-6

Understanding tolerance: In many real-world datasets, numeric values that should be equal differ slightly because of rounding, measurement error, or floating-point representation. RuleSet uses tolerance to determine whether two numbers are close enough to be treated as equal — two values are equal when the absolute difference between them is less than or equal to the specified tolerance:

               reference value
                     │
                     ▼
───────────────┬─────●─────┬───────────────
               │           │
     reference - t     reference + t

          <------ tolerance ------>

              ▲
         test value

If the test value lies anywhere inside the interval,
the comparison succeeds.

abs(test - reference) <= tolerance

docs.title: The Log File
docs.text:
Every ruleset-engine run produces a log file (named YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_ruleset.log) with three levels of output:

  • Info — Informational messages indicating successful operations and summary details:
  • Confirmation of successful parsing of rules and data files.
  • Summary statistics of the data table, including row and column counts, and counts of missing values.
  • Notifications that all validation rules have passed without issues.
  • Warning — Potential issues that don't halt execution but could affect validation accuracy:
  • Columns listed in the rules file without associated value rules.
  • Value rules defined for columns not included in the column list.
  • Absence of any value rules in the rules file.
  • Mismatch between column names in the rules file and the data file, preventing evaluation based on column order.
  • Error — Critical issues that prevent validation from proceeding correctly:
  • Invalid or inaccessible file paths for the rules or data file.
  • Errors encountered while parsing the rules file.
  • Failures during column-level, value-level, or conditional-rule validation (see Section 4 for what happens when the data file itself can't be read).

docs.title: Rule Blocks
docs.text:
If a group of columns share the same rules, RuleSet lets you define those rules once and apply them to the entire group, rather than repeating the same value rules under separate column: blocks. Multiple rule blocks may be specified in one rules file, and columns can still have additional rules defined individually elsewhere.

Syntax:

ruleblock: [<ColumnName_1>, <ColumnName_2>...<ColumnName_n>]
<ValueRule1>
<ValueRule2>
...

Example:

ruleblock: [ "First_Name", "Last_Name", "City" ]
has value type string
has min length 3
is required

docs.title: Value Rules
docs.text:
Apply one or more value-level constraints to a specific column.

Block Syntax:

column: <ColumnName>
<ValueRule1>
<ValueRule2>
    …

Example:

column: 'age'
has value type integer
is >= 0
is <= 120

docs.title: Data Type & Format
docs.text:
has value type <ValueType>

has value type string

Accepted value types:

Value Type Description string Text-based data (e.g., names, addresses, categories). integer Whole numbers without decimal points (e.g., 1, 42, -10). floating point Decimal numbers (e.g., 3.14, -0.01, 2.718). boolean True/False values (e.g., true, false). date-time Date or timestamp values (e.g., 2023-12-25, 2025-03-27T14:00:00). See supported formats below. scientific Numbers expressed in scientific notation (e.g., 1.23e-4). complex Complex numbers with real and imaginary parts (e.g., 3+4j).

has format <FormatType>

has format "YYYY-MM-DD"

Applies only to the date-time type. Supported date-time formats:

["HH:mm:ss", "HH:mm", "hh:mm:ss AM/PM", "hh:mm AM/PM", "HHmmss", "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss",
"YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss", "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm", "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm", "DD/MM/YYYY HH:mm:ss",
"MM-DD-YYYY hh:mm:ss AM/PM", "YYYY/MM/DD HH:mm:ss", "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ",
"YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss+hh:mm", "YYYY-MM-DD", "MM-DD-YYYY", "DD-MM-YYYY", "YYYY/MM/DD",
"MM/DD/YYYY", "DD/MM/YYYY", "YYYY.MM.DD", "MM.DD.YYYY", "DD.MM.YYYY", "YYYYMMDD", "YYYY"]

Other formats for geolocation and currency data will be added in future.

docs.title: Presence & Uniqueness
docs.text:
is required

is required

is unique

is unique

is null / is not null

is null
is not null

docs.title: Pattern & Membership
docs.text:
has pattern /…/

has pattern /^[A-Z]{2}\d{4}$/

is in [ … ] / is not in [ … ]

is in ['Active', 'Pending', 'Closed']
is not in ['Cancelled', 'Deleted']

docs.title: Exact Value Comparisons
docs.text:
is "<string>" / is not "<string>"

is "USA"
is not "N/A"

is == <NUMBER> / is != <NUMBER>

is == 100
is != 0

docs.title: Numeric Bounds
docs.text:
is > <NUMBER> / is < <NUMBER>

is > 0
is < 100

is >= <NUMBER> / is <= <NUMBER>

is >= 0
is <= 120

Local tolerance: is ==, is !=, and the bound comparisons above respect tolerance (see Section 5.1 for how tolerance works). You can set a tolerance local to one column's comparisons, which takes precedence over any global tolerance:

set tolerance at 0.0000001
set tolerance at 1E-06

docs.title: Length Constraints
docs.text:
has length <INT>

has length 5

has min length <INT> / has max length <INT>

has min length 3
has max length 10

docs.title: String Affixes & Substrings
docs.text:
starts with "<string>" / ends with "<string>"

starts with "ABC"
ends with ".csv"

includes "<string>" / does not include "<string>"

includes "urgent"
does not include "spam"

docs.title: Precision Rules
docs.text:
has <INT> significant digits

has 3 significant digits

has <INT> decimal places

has 2 decimal places
